questions.text: What is the significance of the proverb 'Ti akuko adiye bako laye, awon egbe re a gbalorun' ('If a cock crows on earth, its peers in heaven respond') in the play?
options: It is a prayer for good harvest.
Ajanaku uses this Yoruba invocation to challenge the council of chiefs to give his tyranny unconditional support.
It is a children's song.
It describes the behavior of birds.
questions.explanation: Ajanaku uses this Yoruba invocation to challenge the council of chiefs to give his tyranny unconditional support, illustrating his manipulative use of traditional rhetoric.

questions.text: Who is the author of 'Once Upon an Elephant'?
options: Wole Soyinka
Bosede Ademilua-Afolayan
Femi Osofisan
Ola Rotimi
questions.explanation: Bosede Ademilua-Afolayan is the author of the play, which is listed on the WAEC Literature-in-English syllabus for 2026-2030.

questions.text: What is the full birth name of the character who becomes King Ajanaku?
options: Olaniyonu
Odejimi
Ogundele
Odekunle
questions.explanation: Olaniyonu is the birth name of Ajanaku, the illegitimate son of Serubawon and Adebisi who is falsely presented as King Akinjobi's son.

questions.text: What does the name 'Ajanaku' mean in Yoruba?
options: Lion
Elephant
Tiger
Buffalo
questions.explanation: Ajanaku is the Yoruba word for elephant, symbolizing immense power and the arrogance that comes with it.

questions.text: What is the name of the ritual that Ajanaku undergoes in his quest for immortality?
options: Olubori
Ijedodo
Egungun
Ifa
questions.explanation: The Ijedodo ritual requires the blood of virgins to sustain the king's life and grant him immortality.

questions.text: What does the Ijedodo ritual require as a sacrifice?
options: A goat
The blood of virgins
A white ram
Gold and silver
questions.explanation: The Ijedodo charm feeds on the blood of virgins, who are raped and die slow, painful deaths.

questions.text: Who is Desola, and why is she significant in the play?
options: She is the queen.
She is Serubawon's daughter and the sixth virgin victim of the Ijedodo ritual.
She is Iya Agba's granddaughter.
She is a market trader.
questions.explanation: Desola is Serubawon's only daughter. Her selection as the final virgin for the Ijedodo ritual represents tragic irony and poetic justice.

questions.text: What happens to Serubawon at the end of the play?
options: He becomes the new king.
He is pardoned by the community.
He commits suicide after being exposed.
He flees to another village.
questions.explanation: Serubawon commits suicide after his role in the corruption and tyranny is exposed, representing the playwright's verdict on those who trade integrity for power.

questions.text: What is the primary source of the play's stylistic inspiration?
options: Western theatre traditions.
Yoruba oral traditions, including proverbs, folktales, and rituals.
Greek tragedy.
Shakespearean drama.
questions.explanation: Ademilua-Afolayan draws heavily on Yoruba orature, including proverbs, folktales, and cultural practices, to craft an authentic African drama.

questions.text: What is the significance of the play being set in a pre-colonial Yoruba society?
options: It is purely a historical recreation with no contemporary relevance.
It allows the playwright to use Yoruba oral traditions to allegorically critique contemporary Nigerian and African politics.
It celebrates the superiority of pre-colonial governance.
It has no particular significance.
questions.explanation: The pre-colonial setting allows the playwright to draw on Yoruba oral traditions—proverbs, folktales, rituals—to create a culturally grounded allegory about tyranny and resistance that speaks to contemporary African realities.

questions.text: How does the play engage with the Yoruba concept of 'àló' (folktale)?
options: It rejects folktales as outdated.
It uses the folktale form—particularly the elephant and tortoise narrative—as a structuring metaphor for political critique.
It uses folktales only for children's entertainment.
Folktales have no place in the play.
questions.explanation: The play's engagement with 'àló' (folktale) is central: the elephant and tortoise folktale provides the structuring metaphor for the entire political drama, demonstrating how oral tradition can be repurposed for contemporary critique.

questions.text: What does the play reveal about the Yoruba concept of 'ìtàn' (history)?
options: Ìtàn is irrelevant to the play.
The play operates as 'ìtàn'—a narrative that is both historically specific and allegorically universal—to critique power.
Ìtàn is only about ancient events.
Ìtàn has no political dimension.
questions.explanation: The play functions as 'ìtàn'—a narrative that is both historically grounded in Yoruba experience and allegorically universal—allowing its political critique to resonate across time and space.

questions.text: How does the play treat the Yoruba concept of 'orí' (destiny) in relation to Ajanaku's downfall?
options: Orí is fixed and Ajanaku could not have avoided his fate.
The play suggests that Ajanaku's character—his hubris and ambition—determines his fate, aligning with the Yoruba belief that character shapes destiny.
Orí is irrelevant to the play.
Only the gods determine orí.
questions.explanation: The play aligns with the Yoruba belief that character (ìwà) shapes destiny (orí): Ajanaku's arrogant character inevitably leads to his downfall, suggesting that he himself is the author of his fate.

questions.text: What does the play reveal about Yoruba attitudes toward leadership and legitimacy?
options: Leadership is purely a matter of physical strength.
Legitimate leadership requires both traditional sanction (proper succession rites) and moral integrity.
Any strong person can be king.
Legitimacy is irrelevant to leadership.
questions.explanation: The play reflects Yoruba political philosophy: legitimate leadership requires proper succession (which Ajanaku lacks) and moral integrity (which he also lacks), making his rule fundamentally illegitimate.

questions.text: How does the play engage with the Yoruba concept of 'ìwà' (character)?
options: Ìwà is irrelevant to the play.
The play demonstrates that ìwà (character) is the foundation of both personal and political legitimacy, and its absence leads to destruction.
Ìwà is only about outward appearance.
Ìwà has no connection to leadership.
questions.explanation: The play reflects the Yoruba belief that 'ìwà l'ẹwà' (character is beauty): Ajanaku's lack of good character undermines his political legitimacy and leads to his destruction.

questions.text: What does the play suggest about the role of women in traditional Yoruba political structures?
options: Women have no political role in Yoruba tradition.
Women like Iya Agba can wield significant moral and political authority, particularly as truth-tellers and leaders of resistance.
Women are always subordinate to men.
Women only participate in domestic matters.
questions.explanation: The play presents a nuanced view: while patriarchal constraints limit women's formal political power, figures like Iya Agba demonstrate that women can wield significant moral authority and lead resistance movements.

questions.text: How does the play use the Yoruba concept of 'ẹbọ' (sacrifice) to critique political power?
options: Ẹbọ is always portrayed positively.
The play shows how ẹbọ can be corrupted from a sacred practice into a tool of political exploitation and violence.
Ẹbọ has no place in the play.
Ẹbọ is only about animal sacrifice.
questions.explanation: The play critiques the corruption of ẹbọ (sacrifice) from a sacred practice into the violent Ijedodo ritual, showing how traditional practices can be weaponized for political ends.

questions.text: What does the play reveal about the Yoruba concept of 'àṣẹ' (authority/power)?
options: Àṣẹ is purely about physical force.
The play suggests that àṣẹ—the power to make things happen—must be legitimately acquired and morally exercised to be effective.
Àṣẹ is irrelevant to politics.
Anyone can exercise àṣẹ without consequences.
questions.explanation: The play reflects Yoruba philosophy: àṣẹ (authority/power) must be legitimately acquired and morally exercised; Ajanaku's illegitimate and immoral exercise of power ultimately fails.

questions.text: How does the play engage with the Yoruba concept of 'ẹ̀rí' (evidence/truth)?
options: Ẹ̀rí is irrelevant to the play.
Iya Agba's truth-telling and the eventual exposure of Ajanaku's illegitimacy demonstrate the power of ẹ̀rí (truth/evidence) to overcome tyranny's lies.
Ẹ̀rí is only about legal proceedings.
Ẹ̀rí has no political dimension.
questions.explanation: The play demonstrates that truth (ẹ̀rí) is the ultimate weapon against tyranny: Iya Agba's persistent truth-telling and the eventual revelation of Ajanaku's illegitimacy lead to his downfall.

questions.text: What does the play suggest about the relationship between individual and communal responsibility?
options: Individuals bear no responsibility for communal outcomes.
The play suggests that tyranny thrives when individuals remain silent and that liberation requires collective moral action.
Only leaders are responsible for political outcomes.
Communal responsibility is irrelevant.
questions.explanation: The play emphasizes collective responsibility: the community's silence enables Ajanaku's tyranny, and its eventual collective resistance brings him down.

questions.text: How does the play treat the theme of 'ìní' (possession/ownership) in relation to the land dispute?
options: Ownership is irrelevant to the play.
Ajanaku's seizure of disputed land reveals his greed and his confusion between royal stewardship and personal ownership.
The land dispute is a minor subplot.
Only the king can own land.
questions.explanation: Ajanaku's decision to seize the disputed land for the royal house reveals his greed and his failure to understand that royal power entails stewardship, not personal ownership.

questions.text: What does the play reveal about the Yoruba concept of 'ìbá' (kinship/relationship)?
options: Ìbá is always protective.
The play shows how kinship ties—Ajanaku's relationship to Serubawon, the community's ties to the palace—can be perverted to serve tyranny.
Ìbá is irrelevant to politics.
Only biological kinship matters.
questions.explanation: The play explores how kinship (ìbá) can be perverted: Serubawon's parental relationship to Ajanaku drives his corrupt kingmaking, and the community's ties to the palace are manipulated to enable tyranny.

questions.text: How does the play use the concept of 'àdúrà' (prayer/invocation) in relation to political power?
options: Àdúrà is always sincere.
Ajanaku's use of invocation to demand the chiefs' support shows how prayer can be manipulated for political ends.
Àdúrà is irrelevant to the play.
Only priests can pray.
questions.explanation: Ajanaku's use of Yoruba invocation ('If a cock crows on earth, its peers in heaven respond') to demand unconditional support reveals how traditional spiritual language can be weaponized for political manipulation.

questions.text: What does the play suggest about the relationship between tradition and change?
options: Tradition is always good, change is always bad.
The play critiques the perversion of tradition while affirming the value of legitimate traditional governance, suggesting that authentic tradition provides resources for resisting tyranny.
Change is always beneficial.
Tradition is irrelevant to politics.
questions.explanation: The play distinguishes between corrupt manipulation of tradition (by Serubawon) and the legitimate traditional order that Iya Agba and Odejimi uphold, suggesting that authentic tradition provides moral resources for resisting tyranny.

questions.text: How does the play engage with the Yoruba concept of 'àkóbá' (taboo)?
options: Taboos are irrelevant to the play.
Ajanaku's violation of sacred taboos through the Ijedodo ritual demonstrates how tyranny breaks all moral and social boundaries.
Taboos are only about food.
Taboos protect tyrants.
questions.explanation: The play shows how Ajanaku's tyranny involves the violation of sacred taboos (àkóbá), particularly through the Ijedodo ritual, demonstrating that tyranny recognizes no moral limits.

questions.text: What does the play reveal about the Yoruba concept of 'ìjìnlẹ̀' (depth/profundity)?
options: Ìjìnlẹ̀ is irrelevant to the play.
Iya Agba's proverbial speech and the play's layered meanings demonstrate the Yoruba value of ìjìnlẹ̀—depth of wisdom and understanding.
Ìjìnlẹ̀ is only about physical depth.
Ìjìnlẹ̀ has no connection to language.
questions.explanation: The play embodies the Yoruba value of ìjìnlẹ̀ (depth): Iya Agba's proverbial speech and the play's layered symbolism require deep engagement to fully appreciate.

questions.text: How does the play use the concept of 'àwòrán' (symbol/image) to convey its themes?
options: Àwòrán is purely decorative.
The play uses powerful images—the elephant, the generator shed, the fire—as symbols that convey its political and moral themes.
Àwòrán has no meaning.
Only visual art uses àwòrán.
questions.explanation: The play uses powerful symbolic images (àwòrán)—the elephant, the generator shed, the fire—to convey its themes of tyranny, degradation, and destruction.

questions.text: What does the play suggest about the relationship between language and reality?
options: Language merely describes reality.
The play suggests that language—naming, proverbs, rhetoric—actively constructs political reality and can be used to legitimize or delegitimize power.
Language is irrelevant to politics.
Reality is independent of language.
questions.explanation: The play shows that language constructs political reality: Ajanaku's self-naming as 'elephant' attempts to create a new reality, while Iya Agba's proverbs expose the truth behind this construction.

questions.text: What does the play ultimately suggest about the possibility of justice in a tyrannical system?
options: Justice is impossible under tyranny.
Justice is possible but requires collective moral courage and the refusal to remain silent.
Justice comes only from external intervention.
Justice is irrelevant to the play.
questions.explanation: The play's resolution—the downfall of Ajanaku and the restoration of order—suggests that justice is possible under tyranny, but only through collective moral courage and the refusal to remain silent.

questions.text: How does 'Once Upon an Elephant' compare with Wole Soyinka's 'Kongi's Harvest' in its treatment of tyranny?
options: They are identical in every respect.
Both critique tyrannical leadership, but Ademilua-Afolayan uses Yoruba oral traditions and a female truth-teller (Iya Agba) as central to resistance.
They have no similarities.
Soyinka's play celebrates tyranny.
questions.explanation: Both plays critique tyrannical leadership, but Ademilua-Afolayan's play is distinctive in its extensive use of Yoruba oral traditions and its central female truth-teller, Iya Agba, who parallels Segi in Soyinka's play.

questions.text: How does the play compare with Femi Osofisan's dramaturgy in terms of its use of Yoruba oral tradition?
options: Ademilua-Afolayan rejects Osofisan's approach entirely.
Both playwrights draw on Yoruba oral traditions to critique contemporary politics, but Ademilua-Afolayan focuses more extensively on proverbs and ritual.
They have nothing in common.
Osofisan does not use Yoruba oral tradition.
questions.explanation: Ademilua-Afolayan is part of a lineage of Nigerian playwrights, including Osofisan, who draw on Yoruba oral traditions to create politically engaged drama, though her work is distinctive in its extensive deployment of proverbs and ritual.

questions.text: What does a feminist reading of 'Once Upon an Elephant' reveal about the play's gender politics?
options: The play is entirely patriarchal with no feminist dimensions.
The play critiques patriarchal violence (the Ijedodo ritual) while presenting women as agents of resistance (Iya Agba) and complicating simple victimhood (Omoyeni).
The play celebrates male dominance.
Gender is irrelevant to the play.
questions.explanation: A feminist reading reveals the play's nuanced gender politics: it critiques patriarchal violence while presenting women as complex agents of resistance and survival.

questions.text: How does a postcolonial reading of the play illuminate its political critique?
options: Postcolonial theory is irrelevant to the play.
The play allegorizes postcolonial African leadership failures, using the pre-colonial setting to critique contemporary dictatorship and corruption.
The play celebrates colonial rule.
The play has no political dimensions.
questions.explanation: A postcolonial reading reveals how the play uses its pre-colonial setting to allegorically critique postcolonial African leadership failures, particularly the 'sit-tightism' and corruption that have plagued many nations since independence.

questions.text: How does the play engage with the concept of 'the subaltern' in relation to Desola and Iya Agba?
options: The subaltern cannot speak in the play.
Iya Agba, despite being dismissed as 'insane,' speaks truth to power, while Desola's violation is given narrative weight, suggesting the play gives voice to the marginalized.
Only male characters speak in the play.
The subaltern is absent from the play.
questions.explanation: The play engages with subalternity through Iya Agba, whose truth-telling persists despite her marginalization, and Desola, whose violation is central to the play's moral critique.

questions.text: What does a psychoanalytic reading of Ajanaku reveal about his character?
options: Ajanaku is psychologically healthy.
Ajanaku's obsession with immortality and his violent sexuality suggest deep-seated insecurity and a pathological need to prove his legitimacy.
Ajanaku is motivated purely by political ambition.
Psychoanalysis is irrelevant to the play.
questions.explanation: A psychoanalytic reading suggests that Ajanaku's obsession with immortality and his violent sexuality stem from deep insecurity about his illegitimate origins, making his tyranny a pathological compensation for his perceived inadequacy.

questions.text: How does the play compare with Efua Sutherland's 'The Marriage of Anansewa' in its use of traditional African theatrical forms?
options: Both plays reject traditional forms.
Both draw on traditional African performance traditions, but Ademilua-Afolayan focuses on Yoruba ritual and proverb while Sutherland uses Akan storytelling conventions.
They are identical in form.
Sutherland's play has no traditional elements.
questions.explanation: Both plays are on the WAEC syllabus and draw on traditional African performance forms, but Ademilua-Afolayan's play is distinctive in its extensive use of Yoruba ritual, proverb, and folktale.

questions.text: What does a Marxist reading of the play reveal about its political economy?
options: Marxist theory is irrelevant to the play.
The play critiques the concentration of power and resources in the hands of a corrupt elite (Ajanaku, Serubawon) at the expense of the community.
The play celebrates capitalism.
Class conflict is absent from the play.
questions.explanation: A Marxist reading reveals how the play critiques the concentration of political and economic power in the hands of a corrupt elite, with Ajanaku's seizure of land and exploitation of the community representing class-based oppression.

questions.text: How does the play use the concept of 'hegemony' in its portrayal of Ajanaku's rule?
options: Hegemony is irrelevant to the play.
Ajanaku maintains power through a combination of coercion (violence) and consent (manipulation of tradition and bribery of elders).
Ajanaku rules only through brute force.
Hegemony is purely economic.
questions.explanation: The play illustrates Gramscian hegemony: Ajanaku maintains power through both coercion (the Oguno incident, the Ijedodo ritual) and consent (bribery of elders, manipulation of traditional legitimacy).

questions.text: What does a deconstructive reading of the play reveal about its binary oppositions?
options: The play has no binary oppositions.
The play deconstructs simple binaries—legitimate/illegitimate, tradition/corruption—by showing how they are mutually entangled.
Deconstruction is irrelevant to African drama.
The binaries in the play are stable and unambiguous.
questions.explanation: A deconstructive reading reveals how the play troubles simple binaries: Serubawon corrupts tradition, but authentic tradition provides resistance; Ajanaku's illegitimacy is both hidden and revealed.

questions.text: How does the play engage with the concept of 'agency' in relation to its female characters?
options: Female characters have no agency.
Iya Agba exercises significant agency as a truth-teller and resistance leader, while Omoyeni's secret affair also demonstrates female agency within constraints.
Only male characters have agency.
Agency is irrelevant to the play.
questions.explanation: The play presents female agency in complex forms: Iya Agba's moral and political leadership and Omoyeni's secret resistance both demonstrate women's capacity for action within patriarchal constraints.

questions.text: What does the play suggest about the relationship between violence and political power?
options: Violence is always effective.
The play shows that violence—Ajanaku's tyranny, the Ijedodo ritual—is ultimately self-destructive and unsustainable.
Violence is necessary for good governance.
Violence has no consequences.
questions.explanation: The play critiques violence as a foundation for political power: Ajanaku's reliance on violence and ritual sacrifice ultimately destroys him, suggesting that sustainable power requires legitimacy and justice.

questions.text: How does the play treat the concept of 'the common good' in relation to individual ambition?
options: Individual ambition always serves the common good.
The play contrasts Ajanaku's selfish ambition with the community's collective well-being, arguing that legitimate leadership serves the common good.
The common good is irrelevant to politics.
Only the elite matter.
questions.explanation: The play affirms the concept of the common good: Ajanaku's tyranny is portrayed as a betrayal of collective well-being, while the resistance aims to restore communal flourishing.

questions.text: What does a reader-response approach reveal about the play's potential for different interpretations?
options: The play has only one correct interpretation.
Different readers may identify with different characters and themes—some may focus on Ajanaku's tragedy, others on Iya Agba's heroism, others on Desola's victimization.
Reader-response theory is irrelevant.
The play's meaning is fixed by the author.
questions.explanation: The play's richness allows for multiple reader responses: audiences may focus on Ajanaku's tragic downfall, Iya Agba's heroic resistance, or Desola's victimization, each producing different interpretations.

questions.text: How does the play engage with the concept of 'intertextuality' through its references to Yoruba folktales?
options: The play has no intertextual references.
The play's references to the elephant and tortoise folktale create intertextual connections that enrich its meaning for audiences familiar with Yoruba oral tradition.
Intertextuality is irrelevant to African drama.
The play rejects all previous texts.
questions.explanation: The play's engagement with the elephant and tortoise folktale creates intertextual connections that reward audiences familiar with Yoruba oral tradition, adding depth to its political allegory.

questions.text: What does a structuralist reading of the play reveal about its narrative patterns?
options: The play has no structure.
The play follows a classic tragic structure: rise of the tyrant, abuses of power, climax of resistance, and resolution through downfall.
Structuralism is irrelevant to drama.
The play is formless.
questions.explanation: A structuralist reading reveals the play's classic tragic structure: Ajanaku's rise to illegitimate power, his escalating abuses, the climax of collective resistance, and his downfall—following the pattern of classical tragedy.

questions.text: How does the play compare with other African tragedies in its treatment of the tragic hero?
options: Ajanaku is a conventional sympathetic tragic hero.
Ajanaku is an anti-hero or villain protagonist, unlike classic tragic heroes, making the play a distinctive African contribution to tragic drama.
The play has no tragic hero.
Ajanaku is identical to Oedipus.
questions.explanation: Ajanaku is an anti-hero rather than a conventional tragic hero: his downfall evokes justice rather than pity, making the play a distinctive African tragedy focused on the community's liberation rather than the protagonist's suffering.

questions.text: What does the play suggest about the relationship between theatre and social change?
options: Theatre has no social function.
The play exemplifies engaged theatre, using drama to critique tyranny and inspire collective resistance.
Theatre should only entertain.
Theatre is irrelevant to politics.
questions.explanation: The play exemplifies engaged, political theatre: it uses dramatic form to critique tyranny, affirm collective values, and inspire audiences toward moral and political action.

questions.text: How does the play treat the concept of 'history' in relation to 'myth'?
options: History and myth are completely separate.
The play blends history and myth, using the historical setting and mythical elements (the elephant folktale) to create a narrative that is both specific and universal.
Myth is irrelevant to the play.
History is irrelevant to the play.
questions.explanation: The play blends history and myth: the historical setting provides specificity, while the mythical elephant-tortoise narrative provides universal meaning, creating a rich allegorical texture.

questions.text: What does the play ultimately suggest about the relationship between literature and politics?
options: Literature should avoid politics.
Literature can be a powerful tool for political critique, using aesthetic and cultural resources to illuminate and challenge abuses of power.
Politics and literature are completely separate.
Literature has no political function.
questions.explanation: The play demonstrates literature's political power: it uses Yoruba oral traditions, dramatic form, and cultural symbols to critique tyranny and affirm the possibility of collective resistance and justice.

questions.text: Which of the following best describes the genre of 'Once Upon an Elephant'?
options: A romantic comedy.
A political tragedy drawing on Yoruba oral tradition.
A historical documentary.
A domestic drama.
questions.explanation: The play is a political tragedy that extensively draws on Yoruba oral tradition—proverbs, folktales, and ritual—to critique tyranny.

questions.text: What is the significance of the play's title in relation to its themes?
options: It is a random title with no meaning.
It evokes the Yoruba folktale of the arrogant elephant, signaling the play's central metaphor about power and downfall.
It refers to a zoo.
It is a children's story title.
questions.explanation: The title evokes the Yoruba folktale of the arrogant elephant, signaling the play's central metaphorical framework for critiquing tyrannical power.

questions.text: Who is the protagonist of 'Once Upon an Elephant'?
options: Ajanaku, the tyrant king.
Iya Agba, the truth-teller and resistance leader.
Serubawon, the kingmaker.
Desola, the victim.
questions.explanation: While Ajanaku is the central figure, Iya Agba functions as the moral protagonist—the truth-teller and resistance leader whose courage drives the play's resolution.

questions.text: What is the primary setting of 'Once Upon an Elephant'?
options: Modern Lagos.
A pre-colonial Yoruba kingdom.
Colonial Nigeria.
A fictional European kingdom.
questions.explanation: The play is set in a pre-colonial Yoruba kingdom, though its themes resonate with contemporary political realities.

questions.text: Which Yoruba oral tradition element is NOT significantly used in the play?
options: Proverbs.
Folktales.
Rituals.
Written historical documents.
questions.explanation: The play draws extensively on proverbs, folktales, and rituals from Yoruba oral tradition, but not on written historical documents, as it is set in a pre-literate context.

questions.text: What is the function of the Ijedodo ritual in the play's plot?
options: It is a minor ceremonial event.
It drives Ajanaku's quest for immortality and leads to Desola's victimization and Ajanaku's eventual downfall.
It is a comic interlude.
It has no function in the plot.
questions.explanation: The Ijedodo ritual is the plot's central mechanism: it drives Ajanaku's quest for immortality, causes Desola's victimization, and ultimately leads to Ajanaku's downfall.

questions.text: How does the play resolve the conflict between tyranny and resistance?
options: Tyranny prevails.
Ajanaku is killed through collective resistance, Serubawon commits suicide, and legitimate order is restored.
The conflict is unresolved.
External forces intervene.
questions.explanation: The conflict is resolved through collective resistance: Ajanaku is killed during the Jobele ceremony, Serubawon commits suicide, and the community moves toward restoring legitimate order.

questions.text: What is the significance of Iya Agba's exile and return?
options: It has no significance.
It symbolizes the suppression and ultimate vindication of truth and legitimate authority.
It shows that Iya Agba is powerless.
It is a minor subplot.
questions.explanation: Iya Agba's exile and return symbolize the suppression and ultimate vindication of truth: her banishment represents the silencing of dissent under tyranny, and her return represents truth's triumph.

questions.text: How does the play use the character of Desola to critique patriarchal power?
options: Desola is a one-dimensional victim.
Desola's victimization by the Ijedodo ritual exposes how patriarchal systems sacrifice female bodies for male political ambition.
Desola is complicit in her own oppression.
Desola has no symbolic function.
questions.explanation: Desola's victimization by the Ijedodo ritual is the play's most powerful critique of patriarchal power, exposing how systems of male dominance sacrifice female bodies and autonomy.

questions.text: What does the play suggest about the relationship between individual courage and collective liberation?
options: Individual courage is irrelevant.
Individual courage, like Iya Agba's truth-telling, is essential to inspiring collective resistance and achieving liberation.
Only collective action matters.
Courage is not a theme in the play.
questions.explanation: The play emphasizes the interplay between individual courage and collective liberation: Iya Agba's persistent truth-telling inspires and enables the community's collective resistance.

questions.text: Which character represents the corrupt manipulation of traditional religion for political ends?
options: Iya Agba
Serubawon
Odejimi
Desola
questions.explanation: Serubawon represents the corruption of traditional religion and ritual for political ends, orchestrating the Ijedodo ritual to maintain Ajanaku's illegitimate power.

questions.text: What is the significance of Ajanaku's confession about sleeping with the sixth virgin?
options: It proves his innocence.
It reveals his full awareness of and complicity in the ritual's sexual violence.
It shows his remorse.
It has no significance.
questions.explanation: Ajanaku's confession reveals his conscious participation in the ritual's rape and sacrifice of virgins, underscoring his moral corruption and removing any ambiguity about his villainy.

questions.text: What does the play suggest about the relationship between power and legitimacy?
options: Power equals legitimacy.
Legitimate power requires proper succession and moral integrity; power without these is illegitimate and unstable.
Legitimacy is irrelevant to power.
Only physical force matters.
questions.explanation: The play argues that legitimate power requires both proper succession (which Ajanaku lacks) and moral integrity (which he also lacks), making his rule fundamentally unstable.

questions.text: How does the play use the motif of the elephant to develop its themes?
options: The elephant is a neutral symbol.
The elephant represents arrogant, power-drunk tyranny that is ultimately brought down by cunning and collective resistance.
The elephant represents gentleness.
The elephant has no symbolic meaning.
questions.explanation: The elephant symbolizes Ajanaku's arrogant, power-drunk tyranny, which the play shows is ultimately vulnerable to the cunning and collective resistance of the community.

questions.text: What is the dramatic function of the Jobele ceremony?
options: It is a minor event.
It serves as the play's climax, where the tyrant's ambitions are thwarted and justice is achieved.
It is a comic interlude.
It has no dramatic function.
questions.explanation: The Jobele ceremony is the play's dramatic climax: Ajanaku's quest for immortality is reversed, Desola reclaims her life, and the tyrant is killed—the moment of poetic justice.

questions.text: How does the play treat the theme of suicide?
options: Suicide is celebrated.
Serubawon's suicide represents the inevitable consequence of a life built on corruption and deceit.
Suicide is irrelevant to the play.
Suicide is portrayed as heroic.
questions.explanation: Serubawon's suicide represents the inevitable consequence of a life built on corruption, deceit, and the pursuit of power at any cost—the playwright's verdict on such a life.

questions.text: What does the play suggest about the role of memory in resistance?
options: Memory is irrelevant to resistance.
Iya Agba's memory of traditional legitimacy and her refusal to forget are essential to inspiring resistance.
Forgetting is the best response to tyranny.
Memory is only individual.
questions.explanation: Iya Agba's persistent memory of traditional legitimacy and her refusal to forget the truth about Ajanaku's origins are essential to inspiring and sustaining resistance.

questions.text: How does the play use the concept of 'destiny' to explore Ajanaku's downfall?
options: Destiny is fixed and unavoidable.
The play suggests that Ajanaku's character determines his fate, aligning with the Yoruba belief that character shapes destiny.
Destiny is irrelevant to the play.
Only the gods determine destiny.
questions.explanation: The play aligns with the Yoruba belief that character (ìwà) shapes destiny (orí): Ajanaku's arrogant character inevitably leads to his downfall.

questions.text: What is the play's ultimate moral message?
options: Tyranny is inevitable.
Moral integrity, truth-telling, and collective resistance can overcome tyranny, while corruption and ambition lead to destruction.
Violence is always the answer.
Power is everything.
questions.explanation: The play's moral message is that moral integrity, truth-telling, and collective resistance can overcome tyranny, while corruption and unchecked ambition inevitably lead to destruction.

questions.text: Why is 'Once Upon an Elephant' considered an important contribution to Nigerian drama?
options: It is the longest Nigerian play ever written.
It combines Yoruba oral tradition with contemporary political critique, creating a distinctive form of engaged, culturally grounded theatre.
It is the first Nigerian play ever written.
It has no particular significance.
questions.explanation: The play is significant for its innovative combination of Yoruba oral tradition—proverbs, folktales, rituals—with contemporary political critique, creating a distinctive form of engaged, culturally grounded African theatre.

questions.text: Which of the following best articulates the play's treatment of the relationship between power and morality?
options: Power and morality are completely separate.
Legitimate power requires moral grounding; Ajanaku's immorality is inseparable from his illegitimacy.
Morality weakens political power.
Power excuses all moral failings.
questions.explanation: The play argues that legitimate political power requires moral grounding: Ajanaku's illegitimacy and immorality are inseparable, and his downfall results from both.

questions.text: What type of irony dominates the play's treatment of Ajanaku's quest for immortality?
options: Verbal irony only.
Tragic irony: the quest for immortality leads directly to death.
Cosmic irony without human agency.
Comic irony.
questions.explanation: The play employs tragic irony: Ajanaku's quest for immortality, which requires the violation of sacred limits, leads directly and inevitably to his death.

questions.text: Who serves as the play's moral center?
options: Ajanaku
Serubawon
Iya Agba
Odejimi
questions.explanation: Iya Agba serves as the play's moral center, articulating the values of truth, justice, and legitimate tradition against Ajanaku's tyranny.

questions.text: What does the Ijedodo ritual symbolize in the play's political critique?
options: The beauty of Yoruba tradition.
The corruption of sacred tradition for political ambition and the violent exploitation of women.
The power of the gods.
A love charm.
questions.explanation: The Ijedodo ritual symbolizes the corruption of sacred tradition for political ambition and the violent exploitation of women, making it the play's most powerful symbol of tyrannical abuse.

questions.text: What is the significance of the proverb 'The leper said two things of which one is a lie' in the play?
options: It warns against eating contaminated food.
Iya Agba uses it to expose Ajanaku's false claims and pretensions to legitimacy.
It is a prayer for healing.
It praises lepers.
questions.explanation: Iya Agba uses this proverb to expose Ajanaku's false claims and pretensions to legitimacy, challenging his self-presentation.

questions.text: How does the play treat the traditional African value of extended family solidarity?
options: It glorifies extended family as flawlessly protective.
It critiques it, demonstrating how predatory relatives can exploit kinship for personal gain.
It suggests extended family ties are nonexistent.
It claims uncles are always kinder than fathers.
questions.explanation: The play critiques the betrayal of kinship: Serubawon exploits his biological relationship to Ajanaku, and the community's ties to the palace are manipulated to enable tyranny.

questions.text: What does Iya Agba's role as truth-teller emphasize regarding personal ethics?
options: That people should abandon their communities.
That individual moral integrity and courage can transcend fear and challenge tyranny.
That silence is golden.
That only the young can resist.
questions.explanation: Iya Agba teaches that even in the face of overwhelming tyranny, one must uphold moral courage and speak truth to power.

questions.text: What dramatic purpose does Bolaji's monologue in the generator shed serve? (Note: This question refers to the attached literature note, not Once Upon an Elephant)
options: It provides comic relief.
It functions as a classic tragic soliloquy expressing existential despair.
It reveals Makinde's bank account details.
It explains the chemical formula of narcotics.
questions.explanation: This question refers to the attached literature note (The Drama of Taye & Bolaji), not to Once Upon an Elephant. The correct answer for Once Upon an Elephant would be different.

questions.text: What literary device is present when Iya Agba's early warnings about Ajanaku's illegitimacy prove true?
options: Onomatopoeia.
Foreshadowing.
Metonymy.
Anachronism.
questions.explanation: Iya Agba's persistent truth-telling foreshadows the eventual exposure of Ajanaku's illegitimacy and his downfall.

questions.text: Which character represents genuine, disinterested moral authority in the play?
options: Ajanaku.
Serubawon.
Iya Agba.
Odegbami.
questions.explanation: Iya Agba represents authentic moral authority, risking her safety to speak truth and protect the innocent.

questions.text: What constitutes the central dramatic climax of the play?
options: The fistfight between Odekunle and Ajanaku.
The Jobele ceremony where Ajanaku's ambitions are thwarted and he is killed.
The love scene between Odekunle and Desola.
The initial ritual for Ajanaku.
questions.explanation: The Jobele ceremony is the dramatic climax: Ajanaku's quest for immortality is reversed, Desola reclaims her life, and the tyrant is killed.

questions.text: What does the symbol of the 'elephant' represent throughout the drama?
options: Wisdom and patience.
Arrogant, power-drunk tyranny that is ultimately brought down by cunning and collective resistance.
Gentleness and kindness.
The beauty of nature.
questions.explanation: The elephant symbolizes Ajanaku's arrogant, power-drunk tyranny, which is ultimately destroyed by the cunning and collective action of the community.

questions.text: Why is the ending of the play characterized as tragic but morally satisfying?
options: Because evil triumphs.
Because the tyrant and his enabler are destroyed, restoring moral order, though at great cost.
Because everyone dies.
Because the ending is ambiguous.
questions.explanation: The ending is tragic in its cost but morally satisfying in that justice is served—Ajanaku dies and Serubawon commits suicide.

questions.text: What social pathology is critiqued through the character of Serubawon?
options: Urban traffic congestion.
The manipulation of religion and tradition for personal and political gain.
Inadequate healthcare facilities.
High prices of petroleum products.
questions.explanation: Serubawon represents the corruption of religious and traditional authority for selfish political purposes.

questions.text: How does the play depict the relationship between the individual and the community?
options: The individual is always right.
The tyrant Ajanaku places himself above the community, while Iya Agba represents the community's collective wisdom and resistance.
The community is irrelevant.
The individual should always submit to the community.
questions.explanation: The play contrasts Ajanaku's selfish individualism with Iya Agba's communal values, suggesting that true leadership serves the collective.

questions.text: What moral contrast is established between Ajanaku and Odejimi?
options: Both are tyrants.
Ajanaku embodies tyranny and corruption, while Odejimi embodies principled governance and courageous opposition.
Both are heroes.
Odejimi is the villain.
questions.explanation: The play contrasts Ajanaku's tyrannical rule with Odejimi's principled, courageous opposition, highlighting the moral difference between corruption and integrity.

questions.text: What is the thematic significance of Desola's rescue by Iya Agba?
options: It shows that the gods are indifferent.
It represents the triumph of wisdom and compassion over tyranny and violence.
It proves that Desola was never in danger.
It is a coincidence.
questions.explanation: Desola's rescue by Iya Agba symbolizes the power of wisdom and compassion to overcome tyranny and protect the innocent.

questions.text: Which literary term best describes the staged rituals and public performances in the play?
options: Deceptive dialogue.
Spectacle and performance.
Stream of consciousness.
Choric ode.
questions.explanation: The rituals and public performances are spectacles that serve both to reinforce power and to provide sites of resistance.

questions.text: What does the contrast between the legitimate Olubori rite and the corrupt Ijedodo ritual highlight?
options: All rituals are the same.
The distinction between sacred tradition that upholds order and perverted ritual that serves tyranny.
Rituals are meaningless.
Only the king can perform rituals.
questions.explanation: The play distinguishes between legitimate tradition (Olubori) and its corruption (Ijedodo), highlighting how sacred practices can be perverted.

questions.text: What ultimate moral takeaway does the drama offer?
options: That violence is the best solution.
That moral integrity, truth-telling, and collective resistance can overcome tyranny, while corruption and ambition lead to destruction.
That one should abandon family during hardship.
That superstitious beliefs are always accurate.
questions.explanation: The drama champions truth, moral courage, and collective action against tyranny, while exposing the self-destructive nature of corruption and unchecked ambition.
